turns.text: Survey recent Lyman-alpha forest constraints on warm dark matter. How do they compare with sterile-neutrino non-resonant production? Use the sterile-nu tools for production fractions.

**Survey** — 52 tools on 5 servers, 7 read-only probes, 12 papers found.

Warning: the 'sterile-nu tools' named in the task (for production fractions) are not among the available tools. Only arXiv and web search tools were provided, so no production fractions or transfer functions were computed here. Those numbers must come from a dedicated Boltzmann or production code, or be taken from the literature. Lyman-alpha forest flux-power-spectrum analyses set lower limits on the thermal-relic WDM mass that rose from about 0.75 keV (2000) to 3.3 keV (Viel+2013, HIRES/MIKE). Later limits are 5.3 keV from XQ-100 plus HIRES/MIKE (Irsic+2017), 5.3 keV from SDSS DR14 (z<4.5) plus XQ-100 (Palanque-Delabrouille+2019), 3.1 keV from the Cholla suite of 1080 simulations on Boera+2019 data (Villasenor+2022, which weakly prefers about 4.5 keV), and 5.7 keV from high-z HIRES/UVES data with k_max=0.2 s/km (Irsic+2023). All are 95% CL. The main things that loosen these limits are the IGM thermal history (a sudden temperature jump weakens Irsic+2017 to 3.5 keV), peculiar-velocity smearing, patchy reionization, and the choice of k_max (restricting Irsic+2023 to k<0.1 s/km gives 4.1 keV). For non-resonant (Dodelson-Widrow) sterile neutrinos, the standard conversion from Viel+2005 (astro-ph/0501562) is m_s ≈ 4.46 keV (m_x/keV)^{4/3} (omega_dm/0.1225)^{-1/3}. This is my own estimate from memory, not checked against the paper text in this session. Under it, the 3.1-5.7 keV relic limits correspond to roughly m_s ≳ 20-46 keV. That is far above the mass at which DW sterile neutrinos are excluded by X-ray decay limits (this needs confirming; see 1512.05369 and 1702.08430). So pure DW production as all of the dark matter is excluded, and viable sterile-neutrino dark matter needs resonant production, non-standard histories, or a fraction below 1.

Quantities worth checking: DW-equivalent sterile-neutrino mass for each relic limit (3.1, 3.3, 4.1, 5.3, 5.7 keV), using m_s ≈ 4.46 keV (m_x/keV)^{4/3} (omega_dm/0.1225)^{-1/3}; this gives roughly 20, 22, 29, 41 and 46 keV and must be checked against the original paper.; Mixing angle sin^2(2theta) needed for DW production to give Omega_s h^2 = 0.12 as a function of m_s, compared with X-ray decay limits.; Fraction f = Omega_s/Omega_dm produced non-resonantly at the X-ray-allowed mixing, and the mixed cold-plus-warm Lyman-alpha bound on f at that mass.; Average momentum <p/T> of the DW spectrum relative to a thermal one (about 0.9 times the Fermi-Dirac value), which sets the free-streaming length.; Half-mode wavenumber k_1/2 and the suppression at k = 10 h/Mpc for DW versus thermal-relic transfer functions.; How much the relic limit shifts with k_max and with thermal-history priors (5.7 vs 4.1 keV; 5.3 vs 3.5 keV)..

**Plan** — 3 lines of investigation:
1. Use the sterile-nu server to compute non-resonant (Dodelson-Widrow) production fractions Omega_s/Omega_dm and related observables across keV masses and mixing angles. Then locate the DW relic-abundance curve (Omega_s h^2 = 0.12) in the (m_s, sin^2 2theta) plane. — The task explicitly asks for production fractions from the sterile-nu tools. The survey wrongly said these tools are absent: they are in the catalog (serve-sbbn.sh). This direction gives the central quantitative comparison against the Lyman-alpha mass limits.
2. Verify the recent Lyman-alpha thermal-relic WDM limits and their systematic variations from the papers' text, and verify the thermal-relic to DW sterile-neutrino mass conversion. — The survey numbers (3.1, 3.3, 5.3, 5.7, 4.1 and 3.5 keV) come from abstracts. The conversion m_s ≈ 4.46 keV (m_x/keV)^{4/3} (omega_dm/0.1225)^{-1/3} is from memory and must be checked before any DW comparison.
3. Build the X-ray decay and mixed cold-plus-warm side of the comparison. This means X-ray mixing-angle limits at the DW-equivalent masses, the predicted line energies and fluxes, and the published Lyman-alpha bounds on the warm fraction f versus mass. — The conclusion that pure DW is excluded requires the X-ray upper limit on mixing to lie below the DW relic curve at m_s ≳ 20 keV. Fractional DW dark matter then needs the mixed-model Lyman-alpha bound on f, to compare with the fractions from d-01.
Critic's view: revise — The sterile-nu server is serve-sbbn.sh. Its probes (the eV-scale SBL anomaly check, BBN Yp and D/H, N_eff) suggest it may only model thermalized light steriles, not keV Dodelson-Widrow freeze-in. Make step 1 a hard gate. If describe_sterile_nu_tools or a single predict_sterile_nu call at 7.1 keV does not return a non-resonant relic fraction, stop the grid and scan. Report that the production fractions must come from the literature, and do not interpolate a relic curve from outputs that are out of validity.; Add a robustness cross-check. Compare the tool's DW relic curve at 2-3 masses against a published analytic DW abundance, for example the Abazajian/Asaka fits in 1705.01837. Without this, f values tied only to tool calls cannot be verified. Also note that predict_sterile_nu_grid and scan_sterile_nu_parameters overlap; drop the scan if the grid already gives the plane, and save the calls.; This does not fit 13 calls. Six papers, each needing download, chunk reads and cite, plus a post-2023 search, needs about 20 or more calls. Prioritize Viel+2005 for the conversion and 2309.04533 and 1702.01764 for the limits and systematics, all with full text. Take 2209.14220, 1911.09073 and 1306.2314 from abstracts or metadata, flagged as abstract-level. Drop the optional figure step..

**Wave 1** — now exploring, in parallel: Use the sterile-nu server to compute non-resonant (Dodelson-Widrow) production fractions Omega_s/Omega_dm and related observables across keV masses and mixing angles. Then locate the DW relic-abundance curve (Omega_s h^2 = 0.12) in the (m_s, sin^2 2theta) plane.; Verify the recent Lyman-alpha thermal-relic WDM limits and their systematic variations from the papers' text, and verify the thermal-relic to DW sterile-neutrino mass conversion.; Build the X-ray decay and mixed cold-plus-warm side of the comparison. This means X-ray mixing-angle limits at the DW-equivalent masses, the predicted line energies and fluxes, and the published Lyman-alpha bounds on the warm fraction f versus mass..

**Finding:** On the sterile-nu server's DW relic curve (Omega_s h^2 = 0.12), the mixing is sin^2 2theta = 2.545e-10, 3.946e-11, 2.022e-11, 1.084e-11 and 8.81e-12 at m_s = 7.1, 20, 29, 41 and 46 keV. The corresponding radiative lifetimes are 1.6e27, 5.82e25, 1.77e25, 5.85e24 and 4.05e24 s.

**Finding:** At the DW relic mixing, the line energies are E = 3.55, 10, 14.5, 20.5 and 23 keV for m_s = 7.1, 20, 29, 41 and 46 keV. The whole-halo M31 fluxes are 1.75e-3, 1.71e-2, 3.88e-2, 8.31e-2 and 0.107 ph/s/cm^2. The tool's tabulated limits exclude m_s = 7.1 keV (NuSTAR M31 Roach+2020 and XMM blank sky Dessert+2020) and m_s = 20 keV (NuSTAR M31). They report no tabulated limit within 30% in mass at 29, 41 or 46 keV. That means no coverage, not that these masses are allowed.

**Finding:** On the sterile-nu server (DW mechanism), Omega_s h^2 scales linearly with sin^2 2theta and roughly as m_s^1.8. Setting Omega_s h^2 = 0.12 gives a DW relic curve of sin^2 2theta ≈ 8.7e-9 (1 keV), 2.5e-9 (2 keV), 1.2e-9 (3 keV), 4.8e-10 (5 keV), 2.5e-10 (7.1 keV), 1.4e-10 (10 keV), 6.6e-11 (15 keV), 3.9e-11 (20 keV), 3.3e-11 (22 keV), 2.0e-11 (29 keV), 1.08e-11 (41 keV), 8.8e-12 (46 keV) and 7.6e-12 (50 keV).

**Finding:** DW fractions f = Omega_s h^2 / 0.12 from the server: at 7.1 keV and sin^2 2theta = 5e-11, f = 0.196 (Omega_s h^2 = 0.0236). At sin^2 2theta = 1e-12, f = 0.025 (20 keV), 0.030 (22 keV), 0.049 (29 keV), 0.092 (41 keV) and 0.114 (46 keV). At 1e-11, f is ten times these values; 46 and 50 keV then overclose (Omega_s h^2 = 0.136 and 0.158). The free-streaming length is 151 kpc at 7.1 keV, 53.7 kpc at 20 keV and 107 kpc at 10 keV. Delta N_eff is at most 3e-4 and BBN is unconstrained for any DW keV dark matter near the relic curve.

**Finding:** Verified from the text of Viel+2005 (astro-ph/0501562, Eq. 5): m_s(DW) = 4.43 keV (m_x/1 keV)^{4/3} (0.25*0.7^2/omega_x)^{1/3}, normalized at omega_x = 0.1225; the survey's 4.46 keV prefactor is not in the paper but equals 4.43*(0.1225/0.12)^{1/3} = 4.461 keV once rescaled to omega_dm = 0.12. DW-equivalent masses (omega_dm=0.1225 / 0.12): m_x=3.1 -> 20.0/20.2 keV; 3.3 -> 21.8/21.9; 3.5 -> 23.5/23.7; 4.1 -> 29.1/29.3; 4.5 (Villasenor peak) -> 32.9/33.1; 5.3 -> 40.9/41.2; 5.7 -> 45.1/45.4 keV (m_x^{4/3} = 4.520, 4.913, 5.314, 6.562, 7.430, 9.241, 10.182). The survey's range of 20-46 keV is confirmed to within 0.6 keV.

**Finding:** Verified Lyman-alpha thermal-relic WDM limits: Viel+2013 (HIRES/MIKE, z>4) m_x>3.3 keV (2 sigma; 1, 2, 2.5 keV disfavoured at about 9, 4, 3 sigma); Irsic+2017 XQ-100 alone 1.4 keV, HIRES/MIKE 4.1 keV, combined 5.3 keV (2 sigma), falling to 3.5 keV if sudden temperature jumps of up to 5000 K are allowed; Palanque-Delabrouille+2019 SDSS DR14 z<4.5 plus XQ-100 m_X>5.3 keV (95% CL); Villasenor+2022 (1080 Cholla sims, Boera+2019 data, z=4.0-5.2) m_WDM>3.1 keV (95% CL) with a likelihood peak at 4.5 keV and FPS suppression saturating at k>~0.1 s/km from peculiar-velocity smearing; Irsic+2023 HIRES/UVES z=4.2-5.0 m_x>5.7 keV (95% CL, k_max=0.2 s/km), falling to 4.1 keV for k_max<0.1 s/km with earlier thermal priors, with peculiar velocities and inhomogeneous reionization named as the main small-scale systematics.

**Finding:** The mixed cold-plus-warm Lyman-alpha bound of Boyarsky+2009 (arXiv:0812.0010), with masses expressed as non-resonantly produced sterile-neutrino masses, allows any mass in 5 keV < m_NRP < infinity when F_WDM < 0.6 (frequentist 99.7% CL) or F_WDM < 0.35 (Bayesian 95%). The pure-WDM bounds are m_NRP > 8 keV (99.7%) and 12.1 keV (Bayesian 95%).

**Finding:** NuSTAR Galactic Center observations (Perez+2017, arXiv:1609.00667) give, by the abstract's own description, the strongest X-ray line limits on sterile-neutrino mixing over most of 10-50 keV in mass, improving earlier limits by up to about 10x. This is the published limit set that covers the DW-equivalent masses of 29-46 keV, which the server's tabulated limits do not cover.

**Finding:** I made a DW exclusion plot over m_s = 1-100 keV and sin^2 2theta = 1e-14 to 1e-6, from an 80x80 scan (6400 points): 3092 points overclose and 968 are BBN-excluded. The plot shows the overclosure region, the Omega_DM line, the NuSTAR/XMM limits, the Lyman-alpha thermal-WDM bound and the 3.5 keV point. It is Figure 10.

**Completed — Build the X-ray decay and mixed cold-plus-warm side of the comparison. This means X-ray mixing-angle limits at the DW-equivalent masses, the predicted line energies and fluxes, and the published Lyman-alpha bounds on the warm fraction f versus mass..** Partly done: the X-ray limits above 26 keV and the DW-yield check (step 4) are still open. (1) The sterile-nu server does compute keV-scale DW relic densities (answers q-01). Its DW relic curve (Omega_s h^2 = 0.12) gives sin^2 2theta = 2.545e-10, 3.946e-11, 2.022e-11, 1.084e-11 and 8.81e-12 at m_s = 7.1, 20, 29, 41 and 46 keV, with radiative lifetimes of 1.6e27, 5.82e25, 1.77e25, 5.85e24 and 4.05e24 s. The tool flags 20, 29 and 41 keV as 'overcloses' even though Omega h^2 = 0.12, which looks like a rounding quirk. Results are in sterile_nu_grid_DW_e67bfc.csv in the run directory (finding f-001). (2) At those mixings the line energies are 3.55, 10, 14.5, 20.5 and 23 keV, and the whole-halo M31 fluxes are 1.75e-3, 1.71e-2, 3.88e-2, 8.31e-2 and 0.107 ph/s/cm^2. The tool's tabulated limits exclude pure DW at 7.1 keV (NuSTAR M31 Roach+2020 and XMM blank sky Dessert+2020) and at 20 keV (NuSTAR M31). It has no tabulated limit within 30% in mass at 29, 41 or 46 keV, so those masses are uncovered rather than allowed (f-002). (3) The published limits covering 10-50 keV are from NuSTAR Galactic Center observations (Perez+2017, arXiv:1609.00667), which the abstract describes as the strongest over most of that range. Only the abstract was read, so numerical sin^2 2theta limits at 29-46 keV were not extracted (f-008, q-06). (4) For the mixed-model Lyman-alpha bound, Boyarsky+2009 (arXiv:0812.0010, cite-validated in references.bib) allow any m_NRP > 5 keV when F_WDM < 0.6 (99.7% frequentist) or F_WDM < 0.35 (Bayesian 95%). Their pure-WDM bounds are m_NRP > 8 keV (99.7%) and 12.1 keV (95%) (f-007). Pure DW is excluded by the tool's X-ray limits for m_s up to about 20 keV. That rules out the conservative end of the Lyman-alpha DW-equivalent range, but exclusion at 29-46 keV still needs the NuSTAR numbers. Not done: the papers 1702.08430, 1705.01837, 1706.03118, 2007.13751, 2006.09553 and 1512.05369 were not read, so no DW-yield revision was checked. No figures were produced.

**Completed — Use the sterile-nu server to compute non-resonant (Dodelson-Widrow) production fractions Omega_s/Omega_dm and related observables across keV masses and mixing angles. Then locate the DW relic-abundance curve (Omega_s h^2 = 0.12) in the (m_s, sin^2 2theta) plane..** Using the sterile-nu server (serve-sbbn), I ran a DW (non-resonant) grid of 15 masses from 1 to 50 keV times 13 mixings from 1e-13 to 1e-7 (CSV sterile_nu_grid_DW_8d35ed.csv), plus a follow-up grid at the five DW-equivalent masses (sterile_nu_grid_DW_10ad91.csv). On this server Omega_s h^2 is exactly linear in sin^2 2theta and grows roughly as m_s^1.8. Setting Omega_s h^2 = 0.12 gives the DW relic curve: sin^2 2theta = 8.7e-9 (1 keV), 1.2e-9 (3 keV), 4.8e-10 (5 keV), 2.5e-10 (7.1 keV), 1.4e-10 (10 keV), 3.9e-11 (20 keV), 3.3e-11 (22 keV), 2.0e-11 (29 keV), 1.08e-11 (41 keV), 8.8e-12 (46 keV), 7.6e-12 (50 keV) (finding f-003). Fractions f = Omega_s/Omega_dm: 0.196 at 7.1 keV with sin^2 2theta = 5e-11. At sin^2 2theta = 1e-12: 0.025 (20 keV), 0.030 (22 keV), 0.049 (29 keV), 0.092 (41 keV), 0.114 (46 keV). These are ten times larger at 1e-11, where 46 and 50 keV overclose (finding f-004). Free-streaming length: 151 kpc at 7.1 keV, 107 kpc at 10 keV, 54 kpc at 20 keV. Delta N_eff is at most about 3e-4, so BBN does not constrain DW keV dark matter: the BBN-allowed mixing is 1.5e-8 at about 50 keV, far above the relic curve. The server reports no <p/T> or momentum distribution and no per-point Lyman-alpha flag, so the <p/T> question cannot be answered with this tool. The scan scan_DW_d94a06.npz covers 1-100 keV and sin^2 2theta from 1e-14 to 1e-6 (6400 points; 3092 overclose, 968 BBN-excluded). The exclusion plot is Figure 10: /Users/nramachandra/hep-genesis-testing/projects/ramp-combo-lyman-wdm/runs/261019_143114/exclusion_scan_DW_d94a06.png (+ .pdf) (finding f-009). The X-ray-allowed f at each mass is (X-ray limit / relic-curve mixing) and needs the X-ray limits from d-03.

**Completed — Verify the recent Lyman-alpha thermal-relic WDM limits and their systematic variations from the papers' text, and verify the thermal-relic to DW sterile-neutrino mass conversion..** Conversion checked against the paper text. Viel+2005 (astro-ph/0501562), Eq. 5, gives m_s(DW) = 4.43 keV (m_x/1 keV)^{4/3} (0.25*0.7^2/omega_x)^{1/3}, with the omega_x normalization at 0.1225 (tc-...-31; cited in references.bib, tc-...-41). The paper says the masses map one-to-one when the transfer functions match, which assumes a rescaled Fermi-Dirac spectrum. The survey's 4.46 keV prefactor does not appear in the paper. It equals 4.43 keV rescaled to omega_dm = 0.12, since 4.43*(0.1225/0.12)^{1/3} = 4.461 keV. I worked out the DW-equivalent masses by hand, not with a tool, at omega_dm = 0.1225 / 0.12: m_x = 3.1 keV gives 20.0/20.2 keV; 3.3 gives 21.8/21.9; 3.5 gives 23.5/23.7; 4.1 gives 29.1/29.3; 4.5 gives 32.9/33.1; 5.3 gives 40.9/41.2; 5.7 gives 45.1/45.4 keV. The survey's 20-46 keV holds to within 0.6 keV (finding f-005).

Verified limits (finding f-006):
- Viel+2013 (1306.2314, HIRES/MIKE, z>4): m_x > 3.3 keV (2 sigma).
- Irsic+2017 (1702.01764): XQ-100 alone 1.4 keV, HIRES/MIKE 4.1 keV, combined 5.3 keV (2 sigma). Allowing temperature jumps of up to 5000 K lowers the combined limit to 3.5 keV.
- Palanque-Delabrouille+2019 (1911.09073, SDSS DR14 z<4.5 plus XQ-100): 5.3 keV (95% CL).
- Villasenor+2022 (2209.14220, 1080 Cholla runs, Boera+2019 data): 3.1 keV (95% CL), likelihood peak at 4.5 keV. The suppression saturates at k > 0.1 s/km because of peculiar-velocity smearing.
- Irsic+2023 (2309.04533, HIRES/UVES z=4.2-5.0, k_max = 0.2 s/km): 5.7 keV (95% CL), or 4.1 keV with k_max < 0.1 s/km. Peculiar velocities and inhomogeneous reionization are the main small-scale systematics.

Verbatim quotes were cited only for astro-ph/0501562, 2309.04533 and 1702.01764, in /Users/nramachandra/hep-genesis-testing/projects/ramp-combo-lyman-wdm/runs/261019_143114/references.bib. The other three limits come from arXiv abstracts (get_arxiv_metadata) and have not been cited yet. No figures were extracted.

Still open (question q-05): no post-2023 limit was found. The DESI search returned only BAO papers (dead end x-01). It is also unchecked whether 2209.14220, 1911.09073 or 1306.2314 quote their own DW or non-resonant sterile-neutrino masses or an updated conversion such as a Bozek/Abazajian-type relation.

**Critic, wave 1** — continue: 7 findings stand up to the evidence, 2 questioned ('At the DW relic mixing, the line energies are E = 3.55, 10, 14.5, 20.5 and 23 keV for m_s ': The line energies, lifetimes and M31 fluxes are visible in tc-36 to tc-40. The central claim is not: none of the quoted excerpts shows the tool's tabulated limits or the exclusion of m_s = 7.1 keV (Roach+2020, Dessert+2020) and 20 keV (NuSTAR M31). All five excerpts are cut off before any limit comparison. The exclusion statement needs an excerpt that shows the limit values and the comparison verdict.; 'DW fractions f = Omega_s h^2 / 0.12 from the server: at 7.1 keV and sin^2 2theta = 5e-11, ': The claim that Delta N_eff is at most 3e-4 near the DW relic curve is contradicted by the board's own evidence. tc-261019_1-w1-d-03-35 gives delta_neff = 0.001574 at m_s = 7.1 keV on the relic curve (sin^2 2theta = 2.545e-10, Omega_s h^2 = 0.12). The 3e-4 value (tc-24) is for sin^2 2theta = 5e-11, which is 20% of the relic abundance. BBN is still unconstraining, but the stated bound is about 5x too small. The fractions f = 0.196 (7.1 keV) and 0.030 (22 keV) do check out against tc-24 and tc-47.).

Issues: The cross-check against a published DW yield requested in c-01 was not done, and the server normalization looks off. The Abazajian (2005) fit, Omega_s h^2 ~ 0.1 (sin^2 2theta/3e-9)^1.23 (m_s/3 keV)^1.8, needs about 3e-9 at 3 keV for the full relic abundance. The server gives 1.2e-9, a factor of about 2.5 more efficient. The server is also exactly linear in sin^2 2theta, where the fit has power 1.23. The literature result is that DW at the 3.5 keV-line mixing (about 7e-11) yields only about 1% of the dark matter. The server's f = 0.196 at 5e-11 is roughly 10-20x higher. The direction of the overall conclusion likely survives: a lower DW yield means larger relic mixing and stronger X-ray exclusion. The tabulated f values and relic-curve mixings should not be reported as literature-grade until this is reconciled. Note also that the arithmetic itself checks out: 1 keV gives 0.12/1.384e-5 x 1e-12 = 8.67e-9, 22 keV gives 3.32e-11, and the slope is 22^1.8 = 261.; The lifetime values in f-001 are not in its cited evidence (tc-26, tc-35); they appear only in tc-36 to tc-40. In addition, 3 of the 5 points at Omega_s h^2 = 0.12 are flagged 'overcloses', which shows the overclosure threshold is applied with a strict or rounded inequality. Points sitting exactly on the relic curve should not be labelled overclosing in any table or figure.; The verdict on pure DW at 29-46 keV (the Lyman-alpha-allowed masses under the stronger limits) still rests on NuSTAR numbers that have not been extracted (q-06). Without them, the headline 'pure DW excluded' is shown only for the conservative 20 keV end. tc-51 (a two-sterile-neutrino oscillation paper) is irrelevant evidence for f-008..

**Next steps after wave 1** — All earlier directions are closed and none are carried over, so this final wave takes the critic's three suggested follow-ups, trimmed to fit 14 tool calls (about 5, 5 and 4). The highest priority is closing the comparison itself: numerical NuSTAR limits at 29-46 keV and the X-ray-allowed fraction against the Boyarsky mixed bound (q-04, q-06), plus fixing contested f-002. Equal priority goes to the robustness cross-check of the server's DW yield normalization, which could shift f by an order of magnitude, and to correcting the contested Delta N_eff claim in f-004. Lower priority is the mapping-robustness and post-2023 literature check (q-02, q-05), which tests whether the 20-46 keV range is stable. The task does not request facility runs, so no HPC dispatch is needed. Figure 10's limit-set provenance should be documented in the final write-up rather than through a new direction.

New lines of investigation: Extract numerical NuSTAR X-ray upper limits on sin^2 2theta at m_s = 20, 29, 41 and 46 keV. Combine them with the DW relic curve to get the X-ray-allowed fraction f_X(m_s), compare f_X with the Boyarsky+2009 mixed cold-plus-warm bound, and give a final verdict on pure non-resonant production over 20-46 keV.; Cross-check the sterile-nu server's DW yield normalization and its sin^2 2theta scaling against published production calculations. Derive a correction factor and propagate it to the relic curve (f-003), the fractions f (f-004) and the Delta N_eff statement.; Test how robust the thermal-relic to NRP mass mapping is by tabulating paper-quoted NRP-equivalent masses next to the Viel+2005-derived values. Run one targeted search for post-2023 Lyman-alpha WDM limits from DESI P1D or emulator re-analyses..

**Wave 2** — now exploring, in parallel: Extract numerical NuSTAR X-ray upper limits on sin^2 2theta at m_s = 20, 29, 41 and 46 keV. Combine them with the DW relic curve to get the X-ray-allowed fraction f_X(m_s), compare f_X with the Boyarsky+2009 mixed cold-plus-warm bound, and give a final verdict on pure non-resonant production over 20-46 keV.; Cross-check the sterile-nu server's DW yield normalization and its sin^2 2theta scaling against published production calculations. Derive a correction factor and propagate it to the relic curve (f-003), the fractions f (f-004) and the Delta N_eff statement.; Test how robust the thermal-relic to NRP mass mapping is by tabulating paper-quoted NRP-equivalent masses next to the Viel+2005-derived values. Run one targeted search for post-2023 Lyman-alpha WDM limits from DESI P1D or emulator re-analyses..

**Finding:** Comparing mappings from thermal-relic mass to NRP/DW mass (my own arithmetic, no tool used): Viel+2005 Eq. 5 (4.43 keV m_x^{4/3}, omega=0.1225) gives 20.0, 21.8, 23.5, 29.1, 40.9 and 45.1 keV for m_x = 3.1, 3.3, 3.5, 4.1, 5.3 and 5.7 keV. A Bozek+2016-type relation, 3.9 keV m_x^{1.294}, gives 16.9, 18.3, 19.7, 24.2, 33.8 and 37.1 keV. That is lower by 3.1, 3.5, 3.8, 4.9, 7.1 and 8.0 keV, so the DW-equivalent range moves from 20-45 keV to 17-37 keV. The 3.9 keV and 1.294 coefficients come from the direction card. I could not confirm them from any paper text: the abstract search found nothing, and the 2007.13751 abstract quotes no relation.

**Finding:** Of the abstracts checked, only Boyarsky+2009 (0812.0010) quotes non-resonant (NRP) sterile-neutrino masses directly: m_NRP > 8 keV (99.7%, frequentist) and > 12.1 keV (Bayesian 95%). Inverting Viel+2005 by hand, these correspond to thermal-relic masses of about 1.56 and 2.12 keV, which are older and weaker than the 3.1-5.7 keV limits. The abstracts of Irsic+2017 (1702.01764) and Palanque-Delabrouille+2019 (1911.09073) give only thermal-relic masses (5.3 keV for both; 3.5 keV for Irsic+2017 with temperature jumps), so the DW-equivalent values for them come entirely from a mapping relation.

**Finding:** Perez+2017 (arXiv:1609.00667, NuSTAR Galactic Center 0-bounce photons) states in the text that, within the nuMSM, its limit gives an upper bound on the sterile-neutrino mass of m_chi below about 16 keV. The nuMSM allowed band in its Fig. 8 lies between the non-resonant (DW) production line above and the maximum-lepton-asymmetry resonant line below. So the NuSTAR GC limit lies below the whole band, including the DW line, at masses above about 16 keV and up to the edge of its 10-50 keV coverage. Above 50 keV, INTEGRAL limits rule out mixing-produced sterile neutrinos as all of the dark matter. Together these imply pure DW is X-ray excluded at m_s = 20, 29, 41 and 46 keV. This is an inference from the paper's text, not from numerical sin^2 2theta values. The paper notes the limit weakens near 13 and 40 keV ('bumps'), which is a caveat for 41 keV.

Applied to the DW relic mixing at 20 keV (3.9e-11), this predicts about 7e-3 ph/cm^2/s in the NuSTAR 0-bounce aperture (my hand calculation). Numerical flux and sin^2 2theta limits are shown only in Figs. 6-8, which are not machine-readable here.

**Finding:** The sterile-nu tool's X-ray verdicts at the DW relic mixing give only a list of excluding limits, never the limit value itself. At m_s = 20 keV, sin^2 2theta = 3.946e-11, the M31 flux is 0.0171 ph/s/cm^2 and the result is 'EXCLUDED by: NuSTAR M31 (Roach+ 2020)'. At m_s = 29 keV, sin^2 2theta = 2.022e-11 (E = 14.5 keV, tau = 1.77e25 s, M31 flux 0.0388, MW-center whole-halo flux 264 ph/s/cm^2), the result is 'Not excluded by tabulated X-ray limits (within 30% in mass)' with excluded_by = []. So f-002 cannot be backed by a numerical limit from this tool, and its 29 keV 'not excluded' is a coverage gap, not an allowed region.

**Completed — Test how robust the thermal-relic to NRP mass mapping is by tabulating paper-quoted NRP-equivalent masses next to the Viel+2005-derived values. Run one targeted search for post-2023 Lyman-alpha WDM limits from DESI P1D or emulator re-analyses..** I built a side-by-side table of NRP/DW-equivalent masses under two relations (finding f-010). I did the arithmetic by hand; no tool computed it. The relations are Viel+2005 Eq. 5 (4.43 keV m_x^{4/3}, omega = 0.1225; verified in d-02) and a Bozek+2016-type relation (3.9 keV m_x^{1.294}). I took the Bozek coefficients from the direction card and could not confirm them in any paper text: the abstract search found nothing and the 2007.13751 abstract quotes no relation. Treat that column as unverified.

| m_x (keV) | Viel+2005 (keV) | Bozek-type (keV) |
|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | 20.0 | 16.9 |
| 3.3 | 21.8 | 18.3 |
| 3.5 | 23.5 | 19.7 |
| 4.1 | 29.1 | 24.2 |
| 5.3 | 40.9 | 33.8 |
| 5.7 | 45.1 | 37.1 |

Under the alternative relation the DW-equivalent range moves from 20-45 keV to 17-37 keV, lower by 3-8 keV.

Of the abstracts checked, only Boyarsky+2009 (0812.0010) quotes NRP masses itself: m_NRP > 8 keV (99.7%) and > 12.1 keV (Bayesian 95%). Inverting Viel+2005 by hand gives m_x of about 1.56 and 2.12 keV, weaker than modern limits. The Irsic+2017 (1702.01764) and Palanque-Delabrouille+2019 (1911.09073) abstracts quote only thermal-relic masses (5.3 keV; 3.5 keV for Irsic+2017 with temperature jumps), so their DW masses depend entirely on a mapping relation (finding f-011).

The post-2023 search found nothing (dead end x-02). Neither query ('one-dimensional flux power spectrum warm dark matter 2024' or 'Lyman-alpha P1D emulator thermal relic warm dark matter mass limit DESI eBOSS') returned a DESI DR1, eBOSS or emulator WDM limit, only DESI BAO papers (2404.03001, 2503.14739).

Still open: q-05 should be retried with web_search or arxiv_agent using author names; the Bozek+2016 relation needs checking against its source; and I did not check whether 2209.14220 and 1306.2314 quote their own NRP masses. No files or figures were produced.

**Blocked — Extract numerical NuSTAR X-ray upper limits on sin^2 2theta at m_s = 20, 29, 41 and 46 keV. Combine them with the DW relic curve to get the X-ray-allowed fraction f_X(m_s), compare f_X with the Boyarsky+2009 mixed cold-plus-warm bound, and give a final verdict on pure non-resonant production over 20-46 keV..** (The limit curves exist only in figures of the paper's PDF that the figure tool could not extract, and the X-ray tool reports a verdict without a limit value. Numerical f_X therefore needs the PDF figures or the Roach+2020/2023 data, and the tool budget ran out before I could get them.) I could not get numerical NuSTAR sin^2 2theta limits at 20, 29, 41 or 46 keV, so there is no f_X(m_s) table and no f_X comparison with the Boyarsky+2009 bound (F_WDM < 0.35-0.6). Pure DW comes out excluded across 20-46 keV, but only by inference from the Perez+2017 text, not from numbers.

What was established:
(1) Perez+2017 (arXiv:1609.00667; full text in run_dir/1609.00667.txt, tc-...-69, -76, -78). The paper states 'Assuming the νMSM framework, our limit translates into an upper limit on the sterile neutrino mass of mχ ≲ 16 keV'. In its Fig. 8 the upper edge of the nuMSM band is the non-resonant (DW) production line. So the NuSTAR GC limit lies below the DW relic mixing for m_s above about 16 keV, across its 10-50 keV coverage. INTEGRAL covers m_s above 50 keV and is said to rule out mixing-produced sterile neutrinos as all of the dark matter. My inferred verdict is that pure DW is X-ray excluded at 20, 29, 41 and 46 keV. Caveat: the paper notes a weakening ('bump') of its limit near 40 keV, so 41 keV is the least secure point (f-012, medium confidence).
(2) Perez+2017 Eq. 5 gives the flux normalization F ≈ 2.6e-6 cm^-2 s^-1 (m/20 keV)^4 (sin^2 2theta/1e-14) for the default coreNFW profile (J_tot = 29 GeV cm^-3 kpc sr^-1, dOmega ≈ 3.8 deg^2). From this, the DW relic point at 20 keV predicts about 7e-3 ph/cm^2/s; this is my hand calculation (f-013).
(3) The sterile-nu tool returns no limit values. At 20 keV and sin^2 2theta = 3.946e-11 it reports EXCLUDED by NuSTAR M31 (Roach+2020), with an M31 flux of 0.0171 ph/s/cm^2. At 29 keV and 2.022e-11 it reports excluded_by = [] ('not excluded within 30% in mass'), with E = 14.5 keV and tau = 1.77e25 s. That 29 keV result is a coverage gap, not an allowed region. f-002 therefore cannot be backed by a quoted tool limit value; it rests on the verdict strings only (f-014).

What failed: get_paper_figures could not render Figs. 6-8 of 1609.00667, since the HTML has only Figs. 3 and 4 (dead end x-03). Roach+2020/2023 were not checked, and Perez+2017 was not added to references.bib because the budget ran out.

Still open: q-06 and q-07 (numerical limits at 29-46 keV and the f_X table), and q-04 (comparing f_X with Boyarsky+2009).

**Finding:** Abazajian 2005 (astro-ph/0511630, Eq. 7, full numerical DW calculation with the QCD transition, nu_e mixing): m_s = 3.40 keV (sin^2 2theta/1e-8)^(-0.615) (Omega_DM/0.26)^0.5 x {0.527 erfc[-1.15 (T_QCD/170 MeV)^2.15]}. The braced factor is 1 at T_QCD = 170 MeV, and the fit is valid for 135 < T_QCD < 300 MeV. Inverted, this gives Omega_s = 0.26 (m_s/3.4 keV)^2 (sin^2 2theta/1e-8)^1.23. Compared with the server's linear scaling in mixing and roughly m^1.8 in mass, the literature yield goes as mixing^1.23 and m_s^2. The peak production temperature is T_peak ~ 130 MeV (m_s/3 keV)^(1/3).

**Finding:** Literature DW relic mixing from the Abazajian 2005 Eq. 7 (my hand calculation, Omega_DM = 0.26, T_QCD = 170 MeV): sin^2 2theta = 1.23e-8 (3 keV), 3.02e-9 (7.1 keV), 5.61e-10 (20 keV), 3.06e-10 (29 keV), 1.75e-10 (41 keV), 1.45e-10 (46 keV). The server's relic curve (f-003) lies 10.2x, 12.1x, 14.4x, 15.3x, 16.1x and 16.4x lower in mixing at these masses. So the server overproduces DW sterile neutrinos at fixed mixing by more than the critic's 2.5x estimate. The f-001 and f-003 relic mixings should be multiplied by about 10-16 to match this fit. Using Omega_DM = 0.264 (h = 0.674) raises the literature mixings by only about 1%.

**Finding:** Revised DW fractions under the Abazajian 2005 yield, f = (sin^2 2theta / sin^2 2theta_relic)^1.23 normalized to Omega_DM = 0.26 (my hand calculation): at 7.1 keV, f = 0.0064 for sin^2 2theta = 5e-11 and 0.0098 for 7e-11. This matches the literature statement of about 1% of the dark matter at the 3.5 keV-line mixing, whereas the server gives 0.196 and 0.27 (about 30x higher). At sin^2 2theta = 1e-12: f = 4.2e-4 (20 keV), 8.8e-4 (29 keV), 1.75e-3 (41 keV), 2.2e-3 (46 keV), against the server's 0.025, 0.049, 0.092 and 0.114 (50-60x too high). At 1e-11, multiply by 10^1.23 = 17: f = 7e-3 (20 keV) to 0.037 (46 keV), so nothing overcloses. Overall, f-004's fractions are overstated by 1.5-2 orders of magnitude.

**Finding:** Corrected Delta N_eff statement: on the relic curve the sterile number density is fixed by Omega_s h^2 / m_s, whatever yield normalization is used. My hand estimate, assuming one Weyl species and n_s/n_nu = Omega_s h^2 x 94 eV / m_s, gives Delta N_eff ≈ 11.3 eV / m_s while relativistic: 1.6e-3 at 7.1 keV, 5.6e-4 at 20 keV, 2.5e-4 at 46 keV. This matches the critic's 1.6e-3 on-curve value at 7.1 keV, so f-004's 'at most 3e-4' holds only above about 40 keV. All values are 2-3 orders of magnitude below BBN and Planck sensitivity (about 0.2-0.3), so BBN does not constrain keV DW dark matter.

**Completed — Cross-check the sterile-nu server's DW yield normalization and its sin^2 2theta scaling against published production calculations. Derive a correction factor and propagate it to the relic curve (f-003), the fractions f (f-004) and the Delta N_eff statement..** Two success criteria are met (relic-mixing ratios at six masses, revised fractions f with the normalization stated) and the corrected Delta N_eff statement is recorded as an analytic estimate. The cite() step was not done. All numbers below except the fit itself are my hand arithmetic from that fit, not tool output.

At sin^2 2theta = 1e-12, f = 4.2e-4 (20 keV), 8.8e-4 (29 keV), 1.75e-3 (41 keV) and 2.2e-3 (46 keV), 50-60x below f-004. At 1e-11 nothing overcloses.

(4) Delta N_eff (f-018). On the relic curve Delta N_eff ≈ 11.3 eV / m_s: 1.6e-3 at 7.1 keV, 5.6e-4 at 20 keV and 2.5e-4 at 46 keV. **Critic, wave 2** — continue: 3 findings stand up to the evidence, 6 questioned ('Comparing mappings from thermal-relic mass to NRP/DW mass (my own arithmetic, no tool used': The arithmetic is correct: 3.9*3.1^1.294 = 16.9 and 3.9*5.7^1.294 = 37.1. The interpretation that the yield goes as mixing^1.23 is also physically misleading. At fixed mass, DW production is linear in sin^2 2theta for small mixing. The -0.615 exponent of the relic-curve fit encodes the mass dependence (g*(T_peak)) along the Omega = const curve, not a nonlinear dependence on mixing.).

Abstract: It has been realised only recently that TeV emission from blazars can significantly heat the intergalactic medium (IGM) by pair-producing high-energy electrons and positrons, which in turn excite vigorous plasma instabilities, leading to a local dissipation of the pairs' kinetic energy. In this work, we use cosmological hydrodynamical simulations to model the impact of this blazar heating on the Lyman-alpha forest at redshifts z~2-3. We find that blazar heating produces an inverted temperature-density relation in the IGM and naturally resolves many of the problems present in previous simulations of the forest that included photoheating alone. In particular, our simulations with blazar heating simultaneously reproduce the observed effective optical depth and temperature as a function of redshift, the observed probability distribution functions of the transmitted flux, and the observed flux power spectra, over the full redshift range 2<z<3 analysed here. Additionally, by deblending the Lyman-alpha forest into a sum of thermally broadened individual lines, we find superb agreement with the observed lower cutoff of the line-width distribution and abundances of neutral hydrogen column densities. Using the most recent constraints on the cosmic ultraviolet (UV) background, this excellent agreement with observations does not require rescaling the amplitude of the UV background; a procedure that was routinely used in the past to match the observed level of transmitted flux. We also show that our blazar-heated model matches the data better than standard simulations even when such a rescaling is allowed. This concordance between Lyman-alpha data and simulations, which are based on the most recent cosmological parameters, suggests that the inclusion of blazar heating alleviates previous tensions on constraints for sigma_8 derived from Lyman-alpha measurements and other cosmological data. Abstract: We present an analysis of high-resolution N-body simulations of decaying dark matter cosmologies focusing on the statistical properties of the transmitted Lyman-alpha forest flux in the high-redshift intergalactic medium. In this type of model a dark matter particle decays into a slightly less massive stable dark matter daughter particle and a comparably light particle. The small mass splitting provides a non-relativistic kick velocity V_k to the daughter particle resulting in free-streaming and subsequent damping of small-scale density fluctuations. Current Lyman-alpha forest power spectrum measurements probe comoving scales up to ~ 2-3 h^-1 Mpc at redshifts z ~ 2-4, providing one of the most robust ways to probe cosmological density fluctuations on relatively small scales. The suppression of structure growth due to the free-streaming of dark matter daughter particles also has a significant impact on the neutral hydrogen cloud distribution, which traces the underlying dark matter distribution well at high redshift. We exploit Lyman-alpha forest power spectrum measurements to constrain the amount of free-streaming of dark matter in such models and thereby place limits on decaying dark matter based only on the dynamics of cosmological perturbations without any assumptions about the interactions of the decay products. We find that SDSS 1D Lyman-alpha forest power spectrum data place a lifetime-dependent upper limit V_k < 30-70 km/s for decay lifetimes < 10 Gyr. This is the most stringent model-independent bound on invisible dark matter decays with small mass splittings. For large mass splittings (large V_k), Lyman-alpha forest data restrict the dark matter lifetime to Gamma^-1 > 40 Gyr. Abstract: High resolution N-body simulations of cold dark matter (CDM) models predict that galaxies and clusters have cuspy halos with excessive substructure. Title: Unveiling Dark Matter free-streaming at the smallest scales with high redshift Lyman-alpha forest
Authors: Vid Iršič, Matteo Viel, Martin G. Haehnelt, James S. Bolton, Margherita Molaro, Ewald Puchwein, Elisa Boera, George D. Becker, Prakash Gaikwad, Laura C. Keating, Girish Kulkarni

Abstract: This study introduces novel constraints on the free-streaming of thermal relic warm dark matter (WDM) from Lyman-$α$ forest flux power spectra. Our analysis utilises a high-resolution, high-redshift sample of quasar spectra observed using the HIRES and UVES spectrographs ($z=4.2-5.0$). We employ a Bayesian inference framework and a simulation-based likelihood that encompasses various parameters including the free-streaming of dark matter, cosmological parameters, the thermal history of the intergalactic medium, and inhomogeneous reionization, to establish lower limits on the mass of a thermal relic WDM particle of $5.7\;\mathrm{keV}$ (at 95\% C.L.). On the modelling front, we argue that the impact of the thermal history uncertainty on the WDM particle mass constraint has diminished due to improved independent observations. At the smallest scales, the primary source of modeling systematic arises from the structure in the peculiar velocity of the intergalactic medium and inhomogeneous reionization.

Title: New Constraints on the free-streaming of warm dark matter from intermediate and small scale Lyman-$α$ forest data

Abstract: We present new measurements of the free-streaming of warm dark matter (WDM) from Lyman-$α$ flux-power spectra. We use data from the medium resolution, intermediate redshift XQ-100 sample observed with the X-shooter spectrograph ($z=3 - 4.2$) and the high-resolution, high-redshift sample used in Viel et al. (2013) obtained with the HIRES/MIKE spectrographs ($z=4.2 - 5.4$). Allowing for a non-smooth evolution of the temperature of the IGM with sudden temperature changes of up to 5000K reduces the lower limit for the combined analysis to 3.5 keV. Title: New Constraints on Warm Dark Matter from the Lyman-$α$ Forest Power Spectrum
Authors: Bruno Villasenor, Brant Robertson, Piero Madau, Evan Schneider
Year: 2022
Abstract: The forest of Lyman-$α$ absorption lines detected in the spectra of distant quasars encodes information on the nature and properties of dark matter and the thermodynamics of diffuse baryonic material. Its main observable -- the 1D flux power spectrum (FPS) -- should exhibit a suppression on small scales and an enhancement on large scales in warm dark matter (WDM) cosmologies compared to standard $Λ$CDM. Here, we present an unprecedented suite of 1080 high-resolution cosmological hydrodynamical simulations run with the Graphics Processing Unit-accelerated code Cholla to study the evolution of the Lyman-$α$ forest under a wide range of physically-motivated gas thermal histories along with different free-streaming lengths of WDM thermal relics in the early Universe. A statistical comparison of synthetic data with the forest FPS measured down to the smallest velocity scales ever probed at redshifts $4.0\lesssim z\lesssim 5.2$ (Boera et al. 2019) yields a lower limit $m_{\rm WDM}>3.1$ keV (95 percent CL) for the WDM particle mass and constrains the amplitude and spectrum of the photoheating and photoionizing background produced by star-forming galaxies and active galactic nuclei at these redshifts. Interestingly, our Bayesian inference analysis appears to weakly favor WDM models with a peak likelihood value at the thermal relic mass of $m_{\rm WDM}=4.5$ keV. We find that the suppression of the FPS from free-streaming saturates at $k\gtrsim 0.1\,\mathrm{s}\,\mathrm{km}^{-1}$ because of peculiar velocity smearing, and this saturated suppression combined with a slightly lower gas temperature provides a moderately better fit to the observed small-scale FPS for WDM cosmologies.

Title: Warm Dark Matter as a solution to the small scale crisis: new constraints from high redshift Lyman-alpha forest data
Authors: M. Viel, G. D. Becker, J. S. Bolton, M. G. Haehnelt
Year: 2013
Abstract: We present updated constraints on the free-streaming of warm dark matter (WDM) particles derived from an analysis of the Lya flux power spectrum measured from high-resolution spectra of 25 z > 4 quasars obtained with the Keck High Resolution Echelle Spectrometer (HIRES) and the Magellan Inamori Kyocera Echelle (MIKE) spectrograph. We carefully address different sources of systematic error that may affect our final results and perform an analysis of the Lya flux power with conservative error estimates. Adding the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Lya flux power spectrum does not improve this limit. Title: Sterile neutrinos in cosmology
Authors: Kevork N. Abazajian
Year: 2017
Abstract: Sterile neutrinos are natural extensions to the standard model of particle physics in neutrino mass generation mechanisms. If they are relatively light, less than approximately 10 keV, they can alter cosmology significantly, from the early Universe to the matter and radiation energy density today. Here, we review the cosmological role such light sterile neutrinos can play from the early Universe, including production of keV-scale sterile neutrinos as dark matter candidates, and dynamics of light eV-scale sterile neutrinos during the weakly-coupled active neutrino era. We review proposed signatures of light sterile neutrinos in cosmic microwave background and large scale structure data. We also discuss keV-scale sterile neutrino dark matter decay signatures in X-ray observations, including recent candidate $\sim$3.5 keV X-ray line detections consistent with the decay of a $\sim$7 keV sterile neutrino dark matter particle.

Title: Hints, neutrino bounds and WDM constraints from SDSS DR14 Lyman-$α$ and Planck full-survey data

Abstract: The Ly-$α$ forest 1D flux power spectrum is a powerful probe of several cosmological parameters. 1e-10)(m_s / keV)^5. This recipe checks a candidate against X-ray,
abundance and structure-formation constraints.

gives Omega_s h^2 (DW, or SF with a lepton asymmetry), `overcloses`
(Omega_s h^2 > 0.12), Delta N_eff (tiny for keV DM — BBN does not constrain

of Warm Dark Matter (WDM) particles with large free streamin g lengths. We present constraints
on the mass of WDM particles from a combined analysis of the ma tter power spectrum inferred from
the large samples of high resolution high signal-to-noise L yman-α forest data of Kim et al. (2004)
and Croft et al. (2002) and the cosmic microwave background data of WMAP. We o btain a lower
limit of mWDM ∼> 550 eV (2 σ ) for early decoupled thermal relics and mWDM ∼> 2. 0 keV (2 σ ) for
sterile neutrinos. We also investigate the case where in add ition to cold dark matter a light thermal
gravitino with ﬁxed eﬀective temperature contributes sign iﬁcantly to the matter density. In that
case the gravitino density is proportional to its mass, and w e ﬁnd an upper limit m3/ 2 ∼< 16 eV (2 σ ).
This translates into a bound on the scale of supersymmetry br eaking, Λ susy ∼< 260 TeV, for models
of supersymmetric gauge mediation in which the gravitino is the lightest supersymmetric particle.

I. INTRODUCTION
It is now observationally well established that the Uni-
verse is close to ﬂat and that matter accounts for about
(25-30) percent of the total energy density most of which
must be in the form of dark matter (DM) particles. Can-
didates of dark matter particles are generally classiﬁed
according to their velocity dispersion which deﬁnes a
free-streaming length. On scales smaller than the free-
streaming length, ﬂuctuations in the dark matter density
are erased and gravitational clustering is suppressed. The
velocity dispersion of Cold Dark Matter (CDM) parti-
cles is by deﬁnition so small that the corresponding free-
streaming length is irrelevant for cosmological structure
formation. That of Hot Dark Matter (HDM), e.g. light
neutrinos, is only one or two orders of magnitude smaller
than the speed of light, and smoothes out ﬂuctuations
in the total matter density even on galaxy cluster scales,
which leads to strong bounds on their mass and density
[1, 2, 3]. Between these two limits, there exists an in-
termediate range of dark matter candidates generically
called Warm Dark Matter (WDM). If such particles are
initially in thermal equilibrium, they decouple well be-
fore ordinary neutrinos. As a result their temperature is
smaller and their free-streaming length shorter than that
of ordinary neutrinos. For instance, thermal relics with
a mass of order 1 keV and a density Ω x ∼ 0. 25 would
have a free-streaming length comparable to galaxy scales
(λ FS ∼ 0. 3 Mpc).
There exist many WDM candidates whose origin is
ﬁrmly rooted in particle physics. A prominent exam-
ple is the gravitino, the supersymmetric partner of the
graviton. The gravitino mass m3/ 2 is generically of the
order of Λ susy/M p, where Λ susy is the scale of supersym-
metry breaking and Mp is the Planckian scale. If Λ susy is
large the Lightest Supersymmetric Particle (LSP), which
is then not the gravitino, decouples in the non-relativistic
regime and provides a viable CDM candidate. If, how-
ever, Λ susy ∼< 106 GeV, as predicted by theories where su-
persymmetry breaking is mediated by gauge interactions,
the gravitino is likely to be the LSP. Such a light grav-
itino has a wide range of possible masses (from 10 −6eV
up to the keV region). The gravitino – or better to say
its helicity 1/2 component – decouples when it is still rel-
ativistic. At this time the number of degrees of freedom
in the Universe is typically of order one hundred, much
larger than at neutrino decoupling. The eﬀective grav-
itino temperature is therefore always smaller than the
neutrino temperature, and such light gravitinos can play
the role of WDM [4]. Their velocity dispersion is non-
negligible during the time of structure formation, but
smaller than the velocity dispersion of active neutrinos
with the same mass.
Other particles may decouple even earlier from thermal
equilibrium while still relativistic and may act as warm
dark matter. The same is true for right-handed or ster-
ile neutrinos added to the standard electroweak theory.
Since their only direct coupling is to left-handed or ac-
tive neutrinos, the most eﬃcient production mechanism
is via neutrino oscillations. If the production rate is al-
ways less than the expansion rate, then these neutrinos
will never be in thermal equilibrium. However, enough
of them may be produced to account for the observed
matter density. Right-handed (sterile) neutrinos with a
mass of order keV are therefore natural WDM candidates
[5, 6].
The suppression of structures on scales of a Mpc and
smaller, in WDM models with a particle mass of ∼ 1
keV, has been invoked as a possible solution to two ma-
jor apparent conﬂicts between CDM models and obser-

--- Page 2 ---

vations in the local Universe (see [7, 8, 9, 10] and ref-
erences therein). The ﬁrst problem concerns the inner
mass density proﬁles of simulated dark matter halos that
are generally more cuspy than inferred from the rota-
tion curves of many dwarfs and low surface brightness
galaxies. Secondly, N-body simulations of CDM models
predict large numbers of low mass halos greatly in excess
of the observed number of satellite galaxies in the Lo-

parameters which solve all apparent CDM problems si-
multaneously and it is also not clear whether the tension
between theory and observations is due to an inappro-
priate comparison of numerical simulations and observa-
tional data. The main diﬃculty is that the modeling of
the inner density proﬁle of galaxies and the abundance of
satellite galaxies requires simulations on scales where the
matter density ﬁeld is highly non-linear at low redshift.
Furthermore, many of the relevant baryonic processes are
poorly understood.
At z ∼ (2 − 3) the gravitational clustering of the mat-
ter distribution spectrum at scales larger than the free
streaming length of a thermal 1 keV WDM particle is still
in the mildly non-linear regime. At these redshift high-
resolution Lyman- α forest data oﬀer an excellent probe
of the matter power spectrum at these scales. Narayanan
et al. [10] compared the ﬂux power spectrum and ﬂux
probability distribution of a small sample of high resolu-
tion quasar (QSO) absorption spectra to that obtained
from numerical dark matter simulations. In this way they
were able to constrain the mass of a thermal WDM par-
ticle (assumed to account for all the dark matter in the
Universe) to be mWDM ∼> 750 eV.
We will use here the linear DM power spectrum in-
ferred from two large samples of QSO absorption spectra
[11, 12] using state–of–the–art hydrodynamical simula-
tions [13] combined with cosmic microwave background
data from WMAP in order to obtain new constraints on
the mass of possible thermally distributed WDM parti-
cles. We thereby assume that WDM particles account for
all the DM in our Universe and we do not put any priors
on their temperature. We will also further investigate
constraints on the mass of light gravitinos with realistic
eﬀective temperature.
The paper is organized as follows. In Section II we will
describe the eﬀect of WDM on the power spectrum of the
matter distribution. In Section III we will summarize the
method used in inferring the linear matter power spec-
trum from Lyman- α forest observations and discuss the
systematic errors involved. In Section IV A we will derive
a lower limit for the mass of the dark matter particle in
a pure ΛWDM model. In Section IVB, we will obtain an
upper limit for the mass of light gravitinos in a mixed
ΛCWDM universe. Section V contains our conclusions
and some comments on the implications of our results
for particle physics.

We present new measurements of the free-streaming of warm dark matter (WDM) from Lyman-
α ﬂux-power spectra. We use data from the medium resolution, intermediate redshift XQ-100 sample
observed with the X-shooter spectrograph (z = 3−4.2) and the high-resolution, high-redshift sample
used in Viel et al. (2013) obtained with the HIRES/MIKE spectrographs ( z = 4.2− 5.4). Based
on further improved modelling of the dependence of the Lyman- α ﬂux-power spectrum on the free-
streaming of dark matter, cosmological parameters, as well as the thermal history of the intergalactic
medium (IGM) with hydrodynamical simulations, we obtain the following limits, expressed as the
equivalent mass of thermal relic WDM particles. The XQ-100 ﬂux power spectrum alone gives a
lower limit of 1.4 keV, the re-analysis of the HIRES/MIKE sample gives 4.1 keV while the combined
analysis gives our best and signiﬁcantly strengthened lower limit of 5.3 keV (all 2 σ C.L.). The
further improvement in the joint analysis is partly due to the fact that the two data sets have
diﬀerent degeneracies between astrophysical and cosmological parameters that are broken when the
data sets are combined, and more importantly on chosen priors on the thermal evolution. These

arXiv ID: 2209.14220
Title: New Constraints on Warm Dark Matter from the Lyman-$α$ Forest Power Spectrum
Authors: Bruno Villasenor, Brant Robertson, Piero Madau, Evan Schneider
Year: 2022
Abstract: The forest of Lyman-$α$ absorption lines detected in the spectra of distant quasars encodes information on the nature and properties of dark matter and the thermodynamics of diffuse baryonic material. Its main observable -- the 1D flux power spectrum (FPS) -- should exhibit a suppression on small scales and an enhancement on large scales in warm dark matter (WDM) cosmologies compared to standard $Λ$CDM. Here, we present an unprecedented suite of 1080 high-resolution cosmological hydrodynamical simulations run with the Graphics Processing Unit-accelerated code Cholla to study the evolution of the Lyman-$α$ forest under a wide range of physically-motivated gas thermal histories along with different free-streaming lengths of WDM thermal relics in the early Universe. A statistical comparison of synthetic data with the forest FPS measured down to the smallest velocity scales ever probed at redshifts $4.0\lesssim z\lesssim 5.2$ (Boera et al. 2019) yields a lower limit $m_{\rm WDM}>3.1$ keV (95 percent CL) for the WDM particle mass and constrains the amplitude and spectrum of the photoheating and photoionizing background produced by star-forming galaxies and active galactic nuclei at these redshifts. Interestingly, our Bayesian inference analysis appears to weakly favor WDM models with a peak likelihood value at the thermal relic mass of $m_{\rm WDM}=4.5$ keV. We find that the suppression of the FPS from free-streaming saturates at $k\gtrsim 0.1\,\mathrm{s}\,\mathrm{km}^{-1}$ because of peculiar velocity smearing, and this saturated suppression combined with a slightly lower gas temperature provides a moderately better fit to the observed small-scale FPS for WDM cosmologies.

arXiv ID: 1911.09073
Title: Hints, neutrino bounds and WDM constraints from SDSS DR14 Lyman-$α$ and Planck full-survey data
Authors: Nathalie Palanque-Delabrouille, Christophe Yèche, Nils Schöneberg, Julien Lesgourgues, Michael Walther, Solène Chabanier, Eric Armengaud
Year: 2019
Abstract: The Ly-$α$ forest 1D flux power spectrum is a powerful probe of several cosmological parameters. Assuming a $Λ$CDM cosmology including massive neutrinos, we find that the latest SDSS DR14 BOSS and eBOSS Ly-$α$ forest data is in very good agreement with current weak lensing constraints on $(Ω_m, σ_8)$ and has the same small level of tension with Planck. We did not identify a systematic effect in the data analysis that could explain this small tension, but we show that it can be reduced in extended cosmological models where the spectral index is not the same on the very different times and scales probed by CMB and Ly-$α$ data. A particular case is that of a $Λ$CDM model including a running of the spectral index on top of massive neutrinos. With combined Ly-$α$ and Planck data, we find a slight (3$σ$) preference for negative running, $α_s= -0.010 \pm 0.004$ (68% CL). Neutrino mass bounds are found to be robust against different assumptions. In the $Λ$CDM model with running, we find $\sum m_ν<0.11$ eV at the 95% confidence level for combined Ly-$α$ and Planck (temperature and polarisation) data, or $\sum m_ν< 0.09$ eV when adding CMB lensing and BAO data. We further provide strong and nearly model-independent bounds on the mass of thermal warm dark matter. For a conservative configuration consisting of SDSS data restricted to $z<4.5$ combined with XQ-100 \lya data, we find $m_X > 5.3\;\mathrm{keV}$ (95\%CL).

arXiv ID: 1306.2314
Title: Warm Dark Matter as a solution to the small scale crisis: new constraints from high redshift Lyman-alpha forest data
Authors: M. Viel, G. D. Becker, J. S. Bolton, M. G. Haehnelt
Year: 2013
Abstract: We present updated constraints on the free-streaming of warm dark matter (WDM) particles derived from an analysis of the Lya flux power spectrum measured from high-resolution spectra of 25 z > 4 quasars obtained with the Keck High Resolution Echelle Spectrometer (HIRES) and the Magellan Inamori Kyocera Echelle (MIKE) spectrograph. We utilize a new suite of high-resolution hydrodynamical simulations that explore WDM masses of 1, 2 and 4 keV (assuming the WDM consists of thermal relics), along with different physically motivated thermal histories. We carefully address different sources of systematic error that may affect our final results and perform an analysis of the Lya flux power with conservative error estimates. By using a method that samples the multi-dimensional astrophysical and cosmological parameter space, we obtain a lower limit mwdm > 3.3 keV (2sigma) for warm dark matter particles in the form of early decoupled thermal relics. Adding the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Lya flux power spectrum does not improve this limit. Thermal relics of masses 1 keV, 2 keV and 2.5 keV are disfavoured by the data at about the 9sigma, 4sigma and 3sigma C.L., respectively. Our analysis disfavours WDM models where there is a suppression in the linear matter power spectrum at (non-linear) scales corresponding to k=10h/Mpc which deviates more than 10% from a LCDM model. Given this limit, the corresponding "free-streaming mass" below which the mass function may be suppressed is 2x10^8 Msun/h. There is thus very little room for a contribution of the free-streaming of WDM to the solution of what has been termed the small scale crisis of cold dark matter.

arXiv ID: 1609.00667
Title: (Almost) Closing the $ν$MSM Sterile Neutrino Dark Matter Window with NuSTAR
Authors: Kerstin Perez, Kenny C. Y. Ng, John F. Beacom, Cora Hersh, Shunsaku Horiuchi, Roman Krivonos
Year: 2016
Abstract: We use NuSTAR observations of the Galactic Center to search for X-ray lines from the radiative decay of sterile neutrino dark matter. Finding no evidence of unknown lines, we set limits on the sterile neutrino mass and mixing angle. In most of the mass range 10-50 keV, these are now the strongest limits, at some masses improving upon previous limits by a factor of ~10. In the neutrino minimal standard model framework, where additional constraints from dark matter production and structure formation apply, the allowed parameter space is reduced by more than half. Future NuSTAR observations may be able to cover much of the remaining parameter space.

arXiv ID: 0812.0010
Title: Lyman-alpha constraints on warm and on warm-plus-cold dark matter models
Authors: Alexey Boyarsky, Julien Lesgourgues, Oleg Ruchayskiy, Matteo Viel
Year: 2008
Abstract:   We revisit Lyman-alpha bounds on the dark matter mass in Lambda Warm Dark Matter (Lambda-WDM) models, and derive new bounds in the case of mixed Cold plus Warm models (Lambda-CWDM), using a set up which is a good approximation for several theoretically well-motivated dark matter models. We combine WMAP5 results with two different Lyman-alpha data sets, including observations from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. We pay a special attention to systematics, test various possible sources of error, and compare the results of different statistical approaches. Expressed in terms of the mass of a non-resonantly produced sterile neutrino, our bounds read m_NRP > 8 keV (frequentist 99.7% confidence limit) or m_NRP > 12.1 keV (Bayesian 95% credible interval) in the pure Lambda-WDM limit. For the mixed model, we obtain limits on the mass as a function of the warm dark matter fraction F_WDM. Within the mass range studied here (5 keV < m_NRP < infinity), we find that any mass value is allowed when F_WDM < 0.6 (frequentist 99.7% confidence limit); similarly, the Bayesian joint probability on (F_WDM, 1/m_NRP) allows any value of the mass at the 95% confidence level, provided that F_WDM < 0.35.

(2013) obtained with the HIRES/MIKE spectrographs ($z=4.2 - 5.4$). Based on further improved modelling of the dependence of the Lyman-$α$ flux-power spectrum on the free-streaming of dark matter, cosmological parameters, as well as the thermal history of the intergalactic medium (IGM) with hydrodynamical simulations, we obtain the following limits, expressed as the equivalent mass of thermal relic WDM particles. The XQ-100 flux power spectrum alone gives a lower limit of 1.4 keV, the re-analysis of the HIRES/MIKE sample gives 4.1 keV while the combined analysis gives our best and significantly strengthened lower limit of 5.3 keV (all 2$σ$ C.L.). The further improvement in the joint analysis is partly due to the fact that the two data sets have different degeneracies between astrophysical and cosmological parameters that are broken when the data sets are combined, and more importantly on chosen priors on the thermal evolution. These results all assume that the temperature evolution of the IGM can be modelled as a power law in redshift. Allowing for a non-smooth evolution of the temperature of the IGM with sudden temperature changes of up to 5000K reduces the lower limit for the combined analysis to 3.5 keV. A WDM with smaller thermal relic masses would require, however, a sudden temperature jump of $5000\,K$ or more in the narrow redshift interval $z=4.6-4.8$, in disagreement with observations of the thermal history based on high-resolution resolution Lyman-$α$ forest data and expectations for photo-heating and cooling in the low density IGM at these redshifts.

Title: Lightest sterile neutrino abundance within the nuMSM
Authors: Takehiko Asaka, Mikko Laine, Mikhail Shaposhnikov
Year: 2006
Abstract: We determine the abundance of the lightest (dark matter) sterile neutrinos created in the Early Universe due to active-sterile neutrino transitions from the thermal plasma. Our starting point is the field-theoretic formula for the sterile neutrino production rate, derived in our previous work [JHEP 06(2006)053], which allows to systematically incorporate all relevant effects, and also to analyse various hadronic uncertainties. Our numerical results differ moderately from previous computations in the literature, and lead to an absolute upper bound on the mixing angles of the dark matter sterile neutrino. Comparing this bound with existing astrophysical X-ray constraints, we find that the Dodelson-Widrow scenario, which proposes sterile neutrinos generated by active-sterile neutrino transitions to be the sole source of dark matter, is only possible for sterile neutrino masses lighter than 3.5 keV (6 keV if all hadronic uncertainties are pushed in one direction and the most stringent X-ray bounds are relaxed by a factor of two). This upper bound may conflict with a lower bound from structure formation, but a definitive conclusion necessitates numerical simulations with the non-equilibrium momentum distribution function that we derive. If other production mechanisms are also operative, no upper bound on the sterile neutrino mass can be established.

Title: Hints, neutrino bounds and WDM constraints from SDSS DR14 Lyman-$α$ and Planck full-survey data
Authors: Nathalie Palanque-Delabrouille, Christophe Yèche, Nils Schöneberg, Julien Lesgourgues, Michael Walther, Solène Chabanier, Eric Armengaud
Year: 2019
Abstract: The Ly-$α$ forest 1D flux power spectrum is a powerful probe of several cosmological parameters. Assuming a $Λ$CDM cosmology including massive neutrinos, we find that the latest SDSS DR14 BOSS and eBOSS Ly-$α$ forest data is in very good agreement with current weak lensing constraints on $(Ω_m, σ_8)$ and has the same small level of tension with Planck. We did not identify a systematic effect in the data analysis that could explain this small tension, but we show that it can be reduced in extended cosmological models where the spectral index is not the same on the very different times and scales probed by CMB and Ly-$α$ data. A particular case is that of a $Λ$CDM model including a running of the spectral index on top of massive neutrinos. With combined Ly-$α$ and Planck data, we find a slight (3$σ$) preference for negative running, $α_s= -0.010 \pm 0.004$ (68% CL). Neutrino mass bounds are found to be robust against different assumptions. In the $Λ$CDM model with running, we find $\sum m_ν<0.11$ eV at the 95% confidence level for combined Ly-$α$ and Planck (temperature and polarisation) data, or $\sum m_ν< 0.09$ eV when adding CMB lensing and BAO data. We further provide strong and nearly model-independent bounds on the mass of thermal warm dark matter. For a conservative configuration consisting of SDSS data restricted to $z<4.5$ combined with XQ-100 \lya data, we find $m_X > 5.3\;\mathrm{keV}$ (95\%CL).

B. Summary of prior constraints on sterile
neutrino dark matter
Here we describe the current constraints on sterile neu-
trino dark matter. Constraints from production mecha-
nism and structure formation are applicable to models
where sterile neutrino dark matter is produced via either
resonant or non-resonant production, such asνMSM. Im-
portantly, astrophysical X-ray constraints are indepen-
dent of the production method. This discussion lends
perspective on the importance of our result. These lim-
its are shown in Fig. 8.
Constraints from dark matter production: Ster-
ile neutrino dark matter can be produced through a
tiny mixing with active neutrinos. In the absence of
any primordial lepton asymmetry, this is known as non-
resonant (NR) production, ﬁrst proposed by Dodelson
and Widrow [7]. This scenario deﬁnes an upper bound
in the mass-mixing plane, above which too much dark
matter would be produced. However, in the presence of a
large lepton asymmetry, the eﬀective mixing angle would
be modiﬁed by the extra matter potential, and suﬃcient
dark matter can be produced even with a smaller mixing
angle, a scenario known as resonant production, ﬁrst pro-
posed by Shi and Fuller [6] (see Ref. [57] for the latest cal-
culation). In a speciﬁc model, such as νMSM [1–5], the
parameter space is therefore also bounded from below,
set by requiring a suﬃcient amount of lepton asymmetry
to be generated from the model to produce the observed
dark matter abundance. If one is agnostic to the origin of
the lepton asymmetry, but still requires sterile neutrino
dark matter to be produced via non-resonant and res-
onant production, then a more model-independent and
relaxed constraint can be set with Big Bang Nucleosyn-
thesis (BBN) [8], which directly constrains the maximum
amount of lepton asymmetry allowed in the Early Uni-
verse [5]. Moreover, it is important to note that the lower
bound on the mixing angle can be relaxed if sterile neu-
trinos were produced by other mechanisms (for examples,
see Ref. [58–64]).
Structure formation constraints: For some part
of the mass range, sterile neutrinos produced via mixing
can be warm dark matter. They can suppress small-
scale structure formation, which can potentially solve
some of the small-scale problems seen in CDM simula-
tions ([65–67], and see Ref. [10] and reference therein).
Conversely, structure formation can also be used to con-
strain the “warmness” of sterile neutrino dark matter,
which translates roughly to the mass of sterile neutri-
nos. The most robust constraint on the sterile neutrino
mass can be obtain using phase space arguments, re-
quiring mχ & 1.7 keV [68]. A stronger constraint can
be obtained by using satellite galaxy counts [68–71].

I. INTRODUCTION
The nature of dark matter remains one of the most
signiﬁcant unsolved problems in cosmology and particle
physics. The abundance of dark matter has been pre-
cisely determined by observations of anisotropies in the
cosmic microwave background [1], and the measurements
of the growth of cosmological structure in the clustering
of galaxies [2] and in the Lyman- α forest [3]. The fun-
damental nature of the dark matter, however, remains
unknown.
One natural candidate is a fermion that has no stan-
dard model interactions other than a coupling to the
standard neutrinos through their mass generation mech-
anism [4, 5]. Due to their lack of interactions and associ-
ation with the neutrino sector, such fermions are referred
to as sterile neutrinos. Observations are consistent with
sterile neutrinos as the dark matter for a narrow mass
range for the standard production mechanism. In this
allowed range of masses, the sterile neutrino has a non-
negligible thermal velocity component, and is therefore a
warm dark matter (WDM) candidate.
The prevalent ansatz of an absolute cold dark mat-
ter (CDM) component in galaxy formation is not strictly
valid even for one of the most cited CDM candidate, the
lightest supersymmetric particle, which has a small but
non-zero velocity dispersion [6, 7]. The damping scale
at which thermal velocities of the dark matter cut oﬀ
the growth of gravitationally bound structures remains
an open question. One principal challenge to the CDM
paradigm is the order of magnitude over-prediction of
the observed satellites in galaxy-sized halos such as the
Milky Way [8, 9, 10, 11]. Warm dark matter suppresses
dwarf galaxy formation, which may occur through frag-
mentation of larger structures [12]. Semi-analytic galaxy
formation modeling has found that the number of dwarf
galaxies formed in satellite halos may be suppressed due
to the reionization, stellar feedback within halos, and/or
tidal stripping of satellites [13, 14, 15, 16, 17]. Such
semi-analytic modeling is both powerful and malleable,
and must be veriﬁed in robust hydrodynamic simulations
of galaxy formation. Whether a minor or major suppres-
sion of small mass halos is beneﬁcial or detrimental to the
suppression of dwarf galaxy formation remains unsolved.
Four more problems in the CDM paradigm may ben-
eﬁt from the reduction of power on small scales from
WDM. First is the reduction of the prevalence of halos in
low-density voids in N-body simulations of CDM struc-
ture formation, consistent the apparent dearth of mas-
sive galaxies within voids in local galaxy surveys [12, 18].
The second is the relatively low concentrations of galax-
ies observed in rotation curves compared to what is pre-
dicted from the ΛCDM power spectrum [19, 20], which
can be relieved by a reduction of the initial power spec-
trum of density ﬂuctuations at small scales [21, 22]. The
third is the “angular-momentum” problem of CDM halos,
where gas cools at very early times into small mass halos
and leads to massive low-angular momentum gas cores in
galaxies, which can be alleviated by the hindrance of gas
collapse and angular momentum loss through the delay of
small halo formation in a WDM scenario [23]. The fourth
problem is the formation of disk-dominated or pure-disk
galaxies in CDM models, which is impeded by bulge for-
mation due to the high merger accretion rate history in
CDM models, but may be alleviated with WDM [24, 25].
Sterile neutrinos arise naturally in most extensions to
the standard model of particle physics. Singlet neu-
trinos with masses relevant to oscillation experiments
and dark matter can arise in grand uniﬁed models [26],
string-inspired models [27], and models with large ex-
tra dimensions [28, 29]. In reverence to Occam’s ra-
zor, the minimalist model of Ref. [30] produces the

--- Page 2 ---
2
neutrino-oscillation inferred neutrino mass hierarchy, the
dark matter via a sterile neutrino, as well the observed
baryon asymmetry in a neutrino minimal standard model
(νMSM) that introduces Majorana and Dirac neutrino
mass terms to the standard model Lagrangian. There
is also an indication that one or more light sterile mass
eigenstates may cause the ﬂavor transformation seen in
the Los Alamos Liquid Scintillator Neutrino Detector
(LSND) experiment [31, 32]. Another intriguing moti-
vation for the presence of a dark matter sterile neutrino
is abundance of anomalously high pulsar velocities that
may be diﬃcult to produce in the convective hydrodyam-
ics in a supernova, but may be produced in assymet-
ric sterile neutrino emission from a hot nascent neutron
star [33, 34, 35]. However, whether convective overturn
and the resulting global asymmetry in the ejecta alone
can power the observed distribution of pulsar velocities
remains an open question [36, 37].
The potentially beneﬁcial eﬀects of the suppression
of cosmological small-scale structure in WDM can also
lead to observational conﬂicts if the suppression extends
to excessively high mass and length scales. As I shall
show in detail below, the suppression scale monotoni-
cally decreases with increasing sterile neutrino particle
mass. The reionization of the universe by a redshift of
z ∼ 6 requires suﬃcient structure formation at very early
times, and can place one of the most stringent lower-
bounds on the sterile neutrino mass [38, 39]. The ra-
diative decay of the sterile neutrino dark matter may,
however, increase the hydrogen ionization fraction, aug-
menting molecular hydrogen formation, gas cooling, star
formation, and therefore reionization [40]. One of the
best direct measures of clustering at small scales is the
clustering observed in intervening gas along the line-of-
sight to a quasar, known as the Lyman- α forest [41].
Statistically-consistent constraints allowing freedom in
all cosmological parameters and constraints from the cos-
mic microwave background, galaxy clustering, and a mea-
surement of clustering in the Lyman- α forest gives a lower
limit for the sterile neutrino dark matter particle mass as
ms > 1.7 keV (95% CL) [42].
In all studies of the types discussed above of galaxy
formation, cosmological reionization and clustering in the
Lyman-α forest, robust conclusions require an accurate
initial description of the ﬂuctuations arising from the
early universe. In §II, I outline the production mecha-
nism of sterile neutrino dark matter through the varying
particle population in the early universe and the QCD
transition, and describe the resulting non-thermal sterile
neutrino energy distribution. In §III, I follow the evo-
lution of the non-thermal sterile neutrino dark matter
perturbations through the radiation dominated era into
the linear regime of the matter dominated era. This
is related to the CDM perturbation spectrum through
a transfer function. My results diﬀer signiﬁcantly from
previous work on sterile neutrino dark matter perturba-
tion evolution [43, 44] which neglected the eﬀects of the
changing particle population in the early universe, the
QCD transition, and the dilution of the dark matter due
to annihilation.
The sterile neutrino particle dark matter candidate
studied here may be embedded in several extensions be-

partner, or it may have properties that would have it
couple to other species at higher temperatures, including
the inﬂaton. However, knowing its behavior in the early
universe in such extensions would involve introducing a
much more model dependent interaction and production
mechanism, as well as knowledge of all of the degrees of
freedom that are present and may annihilate and dilute
the sterile neutrino in such a model between the coupling
epoch and today. Even in such models with higher en-

of sterile neutrinos negligible upon entering the produc-
tion epoch considered here of T < 300 MeV. The pro-
duction mechanism studied here is a minimalist extension
to the standard model through the neutrino mass gener-
ation mechanism, and does not require what would be at
this point speculation of higher energy physics. There-
fore, the initial abundance of sterile neutrinos entering
the oscillation-production epoch is taken here to be nil.

arXiv ID: 2007.13751
Title: General framework for cosmological dark matter bounds using $N$-body simulations
Authors: Keir K. Rogers, Hiranya V. Peiris
Year: 2020
Abstract: We present a general framework for obtaining robust bounds on the nature of dark matter using cosmological $N$-body simulations and Lyman-alpha forest data. We construct an emulator of hydrodynamical simulations, which is a flexible, accurate and computationally-efficient model for predicting the response of the Lyman-alpha forest flux power spectrum to different dark matter models, the state of the intergalactic medium (IGM) and the primordial power spectrum. The emulator combines a flexible parameterization for the small-scale suppression in the matter power spectrum arising in "non-cold" dark matter models, with an improved IGM model. We then demonstrate how to optimize the emulator for the case of ultra-light axion dark matter, presenting tests of convergence. We also carry out cross-validation tests of the accuracy of flux power spectrum prediction. This framework can be optimized for the analysis of many other dark matter candidates, e.g., warm or interacting dark matter. Our work demonstrates that a combination of an optimized emulator and cosmological "effective theories," where many models are described by a single set of equations, is a powerful approach for robust and computationally-efficient inference from the cosmic large-scale structure.
